Subject: Performance validation: traffic mimicry & bounded-latency methodology

Hi Marissa / Laura —

Thanks for taking our RFP. We have a couple of focused asks as we evaluate inference providers:

1) We need a reproducible methodology for validating a 99th-percentile latency SLA for short-chat prompts (average 40 tokens, max 256). Please include warmup, steady-state, and cold-start definitions.
2) Guidance on synthetic traffic generation to mimic our bursty daily profile (baseline 250 qps, peak 2.5k qps for ~6m bursts) and warm-cache priming strategies.
3) Test artifacts you can provide (scripts, sample workloads, baseline results) and the minimum run duration to reach stable tail latency.

We also want to know what infra you recommend (gpu families, expected concurrency per GPU) and how you measure the impact of batching and KV cache on tail behavior.

Can you share a short validation plan by next week? We may ask for an on-site run or shared lab window if the preliminary results look good.

Thanks,

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
To: Nina Park <nina.park@borealis.com>
Cc: Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-11-02T11:03:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Performance validation: traffic mimicry & bounded-latency methodology

Hi Nina —

Appreciate the clear asks. Summary below and an attached starter load plan (redwood-load-plan.csv) + a latency report template. High-level approach we recommend:

1) Core definitions
- Warm-start: model container has a populated KV cache appropriate to the prompt prefix distribution and worker processes have executed at least N warm-up requests per GPU (we recommend 500-1,000).
- Cold-start: container or model variant swap requiring codec/kernel init; measured separately and excluded from steady-state SLA.
- Steady-state: 15m window after warm-up where throughput and latency metrics converge (variance < 5% for median).

2) Traffic mimicry and burst modeling
- Use a hybrid workload: baseline poisson for steady background + scheduled bursts (sawtooth with 6m holds) to match your 250->2.5k qps profile.
- Include request size mix: 60% short (avg 40 tokens), 30% mid (80–160 tokens), 10% long (160–256).
- KV cache priming: run prefix-probing stage (10–15 min) with representative user prefixes; capture KV-hit ratio target we expect (>65% for chat).

3) Measurement & metrics (what we provide)
- Per-request fields: request_id, start_ts, server_enqueue_ts, server_dequeue_ts, first_token_ts, last_token_ts, finish_ts.
- Latency buckets: p50, p90, p95, p99, p99.9, max, plus jitter and CPU/GPU utilization.
- Throughput: sustained qps, successful responses/min, error classification.
- Resource counters: GPU memory/PCIe utilization, kernel variance, number of context switches.

4) Test methodology
- Warmup: 20–30 minutes of ramp + KV priming.
- Steady-state runs: 3 x 20-minute windows (separated by quick health checks) to ensure reproducibility.
- Burst runs: reproduce 6-minute peak bursts at target concurrency at least 5 times across the window.
- Failure injection: graceful degrade tests with 10–20% of workers simulated as slow/failed to validate fallback policy and tail amplification.

5) Infra recommendations
- For production-like pilots: N x H100 or A100 per node depending on model family and precision (H100 recommended for 70B+ models).
- Typical concurrency per GPU: 10–60 concurrent inferences depending on quantization and target latency; we’ll provide an expected QPS-per-GPU curve per model.

6) Batching & KV cache impact
- Batching improves throughput but increases p99 if not bounded — we recommend a capped batching window (e.g., 10ms) plus dynamic backpressure.
- KV cache drastically reduces compute for repeated context; measure p99 with and without cache priming and report hit-rate sensitivity.

Deliverables we’ll attach or share in the lab:
- redwood-load-plan.csv (starter workload + profile timelines)
- latency-report-template.pdf (dashboard and table schema)
- a baseline 5-run summary for a 13B model under a 500 qps steady-state (optional)

Next steps: can we schedule a 1-hour walkthrough next Tue? Also please confirm whether you prefer our hosted lab runs or if you want a joint lab in your environment (we can provide a temporary Dedicated pool for the pilot).

Cheers,
Marissa Cole

Quick technical clarifications from infra/serving:

- Test harness: we typically use a combination of Locust for high-level profile shaping and a lightweight C++ runner for per-request timing (to capture kernel-level variance). We will provide a reproducible Docker image and an executable.
- Model variants: runs should include FP16, int8-quantized (static), and a quantized + kernel-tuned variant; we’ll provide a deterministic mapping of model size -> expected QPS curve.
- Commands (example):
  - ./runner --target-qps 2500 --mix-file redwood-load-plan.csv --concurrency-probe 5 --report /out/metrics.json
- Observability hooks: we will stream per-request traces to your S3/Drive location and provide Kibana/Graph snapshots.
- Environment: recommend ephemeral Dedicated nodes during pilot (isolate noisy neighbors). We'll document GPU type, kernel versions, CUDA/cuDNN stack, and scheduler config.

Also: for burst testing at 2.5k qps we expect ~X GPU-hours depending on model family; I'll send a short table with conservative numbers by EOD tomorrow.

-karthik
Sr. Staff Engineer, Serving Runtime | Redwood Inference
